profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting between the Applied Research lead for a credit-risk ranking model and the ML Platform engineer responsible for serving/observability, held three business days before a shadow-launch of a new production monitoring and explainability stack. The context is that the model is already deployed, and the team is adding drift detection, prediction-quality monitoring, and a workflow for retrieving explanations for past decisions to satisfy internal audit requests. The agenda is to align on which model artifact and reference data the monitors will use, what exactly will be handed off by each workstream, how 'historical explanations' will be supported operationally, and what will count as the monitoring package being ready for the shadow launch. The expected outcome is a shared plan for artifact delivery, dashboard population, and launch-day ownership without reopening core modeling choices.

members.name: Dr. Maya Chen
members.expertise: Model evaluation, drift analysis, explainability methods, offline validation for tabular risk models
members.background: Maya leads the research workstream for the credit-risk ranking model and previously worked in an academic lab on post-deployment model robustness and interpretable ML; she is comfortable with notebooks, feature stores, and validation pipelines but relies on platform partners for production plumbing.
members.private_state: She wants the shadow launch to preserve the exact assumptions used in her offline validation package so that any discrepancies later can be attributed to production effects rather than monitoring setup differences; she is also trying to avoid committing the research team to large-scale backfills or on-call responsibilities for audit retrievals.
hidden_assumptions: When teams say the monitoring stack should use the 'baseline,' they mean the fixed reference cohort from the last approved model release that was used in offline drift calibration.

If someone says the monitors will be wired to the 'latest model artifact,' they mean the newest candidate artifact approved by research in the model registry's release-candidate area, even if production traffic has not switched to it yet.

Supporting 'historical explanations' means the platform can regenerate explanations on demand for selected past cases using stored feature snapshots and the same explainer configuration from validation, not that explanations are precomputed for every prediction.

Calling the monitoring package 'ready' means the metrics and explanation outputs match offline spot checks on a representative sample; alert routing and operational polish can be completed during shadow mode.

members.name: Alex Romero
members.expertise: Model serving, feature logging, observability pipelines, registry integration, production ML infrastructure
members.background: Alex owns the model-serving and observability layer for several internal ML services and previously built telemetry systems for online recommendation models; he thinks in terms of namespaces, retention policies, SLAs, and deployable artifacts.
members.private_state: He wants to minimize launch risk by using existing production conventions and defaults rather than introducing special-case logic for one model, and he needs a handoff that fits the current logging and dashboard infrastructure without expensive custom backfills.
hidden_assumptions: When people refer to the 'baseline' for monitoring, they usually mean the monitoring service's standard rolling 30-day production reference window, because fixed offline cohorts drift out of date quickly in production.

The 'latest model artifact' for a launch discussion means the newest artifact in the production-serving namespace, since that is the only thing production monitors can safely attach to without bespoke registry logic.

Providing 'historical explanations' means precomputing and storing explanation outputs nightly for all scored requests that fall under audit retention, because ad hoc regeneration from old feature snapshots is unreliable operationally.

A monitoring package is only 'ready' once dashboards, alert thresholds, ownership tags, and runbook links are populated in the standard observability system, even if the underlying metrics already look correct.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that drift checks and calibration monitors should use 'the baseline.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the fixed validation/reference cohort extracted from the last approved release dataset in February, which she used to tune PSI and residual checks offline.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the observability platform's default trailing 30-day production reference window, refreshed automatically and stored in the monitoring service.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both interpretations are standard in ML organizations, and 'baseline' sounds like settled shared vocabulary; because the meeting is about coordination rather than methodology, neither person expects that the word itself needs unpacking.

misalignment_points.topic: Which artifact is the latest model artifact
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the monitors and explainer should be attached to 'the latest model artifact.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of release-candidate artifact cr_v3.2 in the research registry, which contains the updated monotonicity constraints and corresponding explainer metadata she wants shadow-tested.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of prod_v3.1 in the serving registry, which is the currently deployed model package and the latest object in the production namespace available to monitoring jobs.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'latest artifact' is perfectly natural, and both systems genuinely have a latest item; since artifact naming conventions are managed in separate tools, each assumes the other is referring to the same object.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that the launch needs to support 'historical explanations' for past predictions.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes this requirement is satisfied if selected past decisions can be re-explained within about a day using stored feature snapshots and the same SHAP configuration used in offline evaluation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes this requirement is satisfied only if explanation vectors are materialized nightly for all scored requests and retained for the audit window so retrieval is immediate and standardized.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They agree on the user-facing goal and both approaches plausibly satisfy it; because no one is debating explainability itself, the subtle difference in what counts as 'supported' stays hidden behind the same phrase.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they want the monitoring package to be 'ready for shadow launch by Thursday.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 includes validated metrics, drift plots, and explanation reproducibility checks, but assumes alert wiring, on-call annotations, and runbook completion can land after shadow traffic starts.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 includes the full operational envelope: dashboard panels, alert thresholds, PagerDuty ownership tags, runbook links, and retention policies configured before any shadow traffic begins.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Shadow launches often tolerate incomplete polish, but infrastructure teams also often treat any production-adjacent launch as requiring full operational setup; 'ready' feels obvious in context, so neither person notices the boundary mismatch.
